title: A short recipe from a huge pantry
allegory: A sparse autoencoder is a taster who rewrites a smoothie as a recipe card: a few ingredients, with amounts, picked from a pantry far bigger than the list of tastes, and the card must remake the same smoothie.

props.label: one neuron: a mess of unrelated things

cap.1: A model knows more ideas than it has neurons, so ideas get crammed together. Look at one neuron and it responds to a jumble of unrelated things.
cap.2: Superposition: features outnumber neurons, so they share them as overlapping directions. The neuron basis is the wrong place to look for clean concepts.
cap.3: With more features than dimensions, features sit on non-orthogonal directions and neurons are polysemantic. You need a basis learned from the data, not the one the architecture gives you.

cap.1: Tasting a smoothie tells you sweet, sour, thick: every taste is a blend of many fruits. A recipe card names the few fruits that went in, from a huge pantry.
cap.2: A sparse autoencoder rewrites an activation as a short list: a few directions picked from a much larger dictionary, with amounts. Those directions are the readable part.
cap.3: Encoder to d_sae = expansion × d_model latents, ReLU, decoder back to d_model. Trained on reconstruction plus an L1 penalty so only a handful of latents are non-zero per token.

cap.1: Two rules pull against each other: remake the smoothie faithfully, and use as few ingredients as possible. λ sets how strict the second rule is.
cap.2: Loss = reconstruction error + λ × the L1 norm of the latents, with f = ReLU(W_enc x + b_enc) and x̂ = W_dec f + b_dec. λ is the single biggest lever you have.
cap.3: L1 is a convex stand-in for L0, the count of active latents. JumpReLU and TopK SAEs enforce sparsity more directly (GemmaScope uses JumpReLU). Either way, L0 is the number you read.

chapters.name: The hidden ingredient
chapters.verdict: The concept was there all along; the neuron basis hid it.

cap.1: In the first big run, one ingredient on the card lit up for Arabic script. Look neuron by neuron and it is simply not there: it was smeared across many.
cap.2: Towards Monosemanticity re-expressed a 512-neuron MLP layer as 4,096 latents. Latent A/1/3450 fires on Arabic script and has no single-neuron counterpart.
cap.3: Bricken et al. (2023): a one-layer transformer, expansion factors 1x to 256x, headline run at 4,096 latents. Scaled later to Claude 3 Sonnet: feature 34M/31164353, the Golden Gate Bridge.

chapters.name: Dead and dense
chapters.verdict: Watch L0, the dead count and the sparsity histogram, not loss alone.

cap.1: Two ways a pantry goes wrong: ingredients nobody ever uses, and one ingredient that goes into everything. Neither helps you read the recipe.
cap.2: Dead latents never fire, get no gradient and are lost capacity; dense latents fire on more than 1 token in 100 and are unreadable. Reconstruction loss alone hides both.
cap.3: Many dead latents with good loss usually means d_sae is too large (an ARENA run used expansion 32 where 16 sufficed). Healthy log-sparsity mass sits around -5 to -3, with no spike at the floor or lump near 0.

chapters.name: The honest state
items: Caveat: sparser is not always clearer
Check a latent by steering with it

cap.1: You will mostly use ready-made pantries rather than stock your own. And a tidier recipe is not always a truer one, so test what an ingredient actually does.
cap.2: Current practice: load pretrained SAEs (Gemma Scope) with SAELens and read Neuronpedia dashboards. Emerging: absorption and splitting mean sparser is not reliably more interpretable.
cap.3: My call: consume pretrained SAEs, report L0 and dead-latent counts, treat every label as a hypothesis and confirm it causally by steering or ablating. That is how SAEs become tools for understanding and steering.

readouts.label: diagnosis
readouts.f: width > 24 ? 'many dead latents: pantry too big, shrink the expansion factor toward 16' : (l1 > 0.8 ? 'dead latents: L1 too strict' : (l1 < 0.25 ? 'dense latents: L1 too weak, unreadable' : 'healthy: most latents fire on 1e-5 to 1e-3 of tokens'))

caption.1: Slide the L1 rule and the pantry size. A spike at the left means ingredients nobody uses; a lump at the right means ones that go into everything.
caption.2: Aim for most latents firing on between 1e-5 and 1e-3 of tokens. Too weak an L1 gives dense, unreadable latents; too wide a dictionary leaves a pile of dead ones.
caption.3: Toy histogram encoding ARENA's diagnostics: a dead spike at log10(ε) from over-provisioned d_sae (expansion 32 vs 16) or a high lr without warmup; mass near 0 when λ is too small.

hamming.what: A wide autoencoder that rewrites one layer's activation as a few active directions from a much larger learned dictionary.
hamming.when: When neurons are too tangled to read, which in language models is almost always, because superposition packs in more features than neurons.
hamming.why: It turns a jumble of polysemantic neurons into thousands of mostly readable latents you can inspect, ablate and steer.
